text.front:
Against ethics in law: the problems with applying ethics and
integrity rules to doctrinal legal scholarship
Gareth Davies
Faculty of Law, Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, Netherlands
ABSTRACT
Legal scholars are increasingly asked to respect research ethics
rules, in particular those concerning conflicts of interest, following
a trend begun in social sciences after its crises of replication.
However, whereas empirical science needs trust, because it rests
on potentially falsifiable data, doctrinal legal scholarship consists
of arguments which cannot be faked. It is all on the page. The
quality of legal scholarship is served by encouraging readers to
engage with what is written as robustly as possible, rather than
to consider the integrity of the person who wrote it. The ad
hominem path moreover leads to incoherent distinctions
between people committed to a view for financial or career
reasons, and those committed for ideological ones. Both can
narrow the mind of the writer and reduce the quality of their
output (although the claim that a good argument cannot be
made for payment is a surprising one to hear from lawyers).
However, the better response is not to try and get inside the
author's motivations, but to read their words and challenge them.
Rules on scholarly conflicts of interests are a distraction from the
necessary sceptical and robust engagement with texts.
KEYWORDS
Research ethics; research
integrity; legal method;
empirical legal studies
text.body:
Introduction
A wave of ethics is sweeping over universities and research institutions, in the form of
codes of conduct and integrity to which the institutions and the researchers are expected
to adhere. 1 The immediate cause is a crisis of trust in research, particularly social science
and psychological research, and the major aim is to restore that trust and with it the
status of researchers. Lawyers and law schools, as part of their ongoing struggle to be
taken seriously as part of the genuinely scientific community, 2 and as a community

text.body:
just as interested in status as their academic peers, are embracing this ethical turn on the
whole uncritically -after all, what's wrong with promising to be honest and fair?
However, the role of integrity in research differs according to the nature of the
research. 3 The data on which most empirical social science and psychological research
relies is not, in the short term, checkable by the reader, so that trust in individual
researchers plays an important role in the acceptance of their results. 4 By contrast,
legal scholarship, of the more traditional, non-empirical, kind, providing critical analysis
of judgments, legislation and legal developments, does not rely on data beyond what is
presented in the writing or is publicly available. 5 Everything is, or should be, on the
page. There is no need to accept a legal argument because the person making it is
respected, because all the ingredients for a critical analysis of its value are there, dis-
played, for the reader. The merits of legal scholarship can, and should, be judged,
without regard to who produced it or their motivations.
A system aimed at promoting and displaying the moral virtues of legal scholars under-
mines this process. 6 It is irrelevant to the scholarship itself, but in encouraging personal
status-based judgments it crowds out the critical reading that is the basis of legal scholar-
ship's value and progress. 7 We should not want law professors to be eminent figures
beyond reproach whose word is taken on trust. We should want them to be mere
authors, whose personal characteristics are quite irrelevant to someone reviewing their
work. Let them be corrupt, amoral, ethically blind. Sometimes from twisted minds
come interesting thoughts. 8 The world of legal scholarship does not need deep normative
conformity. It needs challenging ideas, expressed in rigorous argument. It needs dissent
far more than it needs consensus. 9
This makes the application of at least some of the rules usually found in research codes -
those on general 'integrity', and those on conflicts of interests -positively harmful when
applied to doctrinal legal scholars. The financial and institutional commitments on which
conflicts rules focus are no different in their effects on scholarship than the normative com-
mitments which are ubiquitous, even celebrated. The only difference between working for
migrant rights and for corporations is who one serves. Transparency about external interests
creates a false hierarchy of trustability, and like the general integrity rule, serves above all to
promote the assessment of research according to the motivations and character of the
researcher, putting ad hominem arguments above engagement with content.
This article attempts to make the argument above. It begins with an overview of the
'turn to ethics' and some of the reasons why this is occurring, and the critiques that
are being made. It then explains why law is different, and why the logic of integrity
which applies to empirical scientists does not apply to legal scholars. Some will feel
that my argument is naïve, and the process of pure reasoning and debate which I
plead for is utopian. In reality the public are not all scholars and cannot engage critically
in the way I suggest. Society does, it might seem, then need to know and control the

4 Torsten Wilholt. 'Epistemic Trust in Science' (2013) 24(2) British Journal for the Philosophy of Science 233; Felipe Romero,
'Philosophy of Science and the Replicability Crisis' (2019) Philosophy Compass 14:e12633.
5 Jan Smits, The Mind and Method Of The Legal Academic (Edward Elgar 2012).
6 See Kenneth Rothman, 'Conflict of Interest: The New McCarthyism in Science' (1993) 269(21) JAMA 2782.
7 Patrick Bondy, 'Virtues, Evidence, and Ad Hominem Arguments' (2015) 35(4) Informal Logic 450.
8 c.f. Bruce Macfarlane, Researching with Integrity: The Ethics of Academic Enquiry (Routledge 2009).
9 Edward Rubin, 'On beyond Truth: A Theory for Evaluating Legal Scholarship' (1992) 80 California Law Review 889.
text.body:
influences and commitments to which legal scholars are subject. In the final section, the
article considers why such a concession to reality would be regressive. Even if personal
status does, in reality, play a role in law, that should be confronted, not embraced.
The argument is based around the practice of academic law in continental Europe and
the UK, where the research that lawyers do has been undergoing significant change over
the past two decades as the result of the rise of empirical legal studies, and the intellectual,
institutional and normative changes that it brings, such as the codes under discussion
here. 10 Within the United States similar processes have been ongoing for longer. 11
However, while the contemporary relevance of the arguments made may be greater in
some jurisdictions than others, most of the discussion of integrity rules and conflicts
of interests is general in nature, and would apply wherever academic lawyers do tra-
ditional doctrinal research.
The turn to ethics
It is not uncommon for states or funding bodies to have codes of conduct for research,
laying out obligations of integrity and good practice, to which institutions and researchers
are expected to adhere. 12 There may also be an element of symbolic obeisance involved,
perhaps the signing of the code by the researcher who has received an award, or, in the
case of the Netherlands, by all those who receive a PhD. 13 There are also practical, insti-
tutional components, such as the setting up of ethics bodies, procedures for assessing
research plans and for addressing claims of misconduct, and also educational programmes,
such as compulsory courses in research ethics for young researchers.
The idea of ethics in research is not new, and often traced back to abhorrent eugenic or
other medical experiments. 14 The recent resurgence is primarily to do with scandals in
the social and psychological sciences, whereby prominent figures were accused of falsify-
ing data, or at least not following correct procedures, and high-profile results that were
already widely reported and cited were cast into doubt. 15 Systematic investigations into
why and how this happened produced the phrase 'the crisis of replicability', expressing
the fear that much, perhaps most, impactful research in vulnerable fields could not in
fact be replicated -suggesting it may not have been correct, and raising doubts about

text.body:
how the results were obtained in the first place. 16 Can the headline grabbing research on
behaviour, management, psychology, and politics, and the other soft empirical fields be
believed at all?
A number of factors drove the crisis. Perhaps most simply, a world with no shortage of
social, political and economic problems, and an endless hunger for efficiency, profit, and
happiness, provides a grateful market for research which seems to promise insight into
these things. Careers can be made with research results which seem to deliver an
answer to a pressing question.
In the textbook explanations of how empirical science works, it is always
emphasised that experiments must be repeated, and a theory is only accepted after
multiple researchers or teams reach the same results. Because things can go wrong,
and because randomness can lead to misleading conclusions, replication is an essential
part of the truth-finding process. However, in the competitive university market it is
hard to make a career repeating someone else's experiments, so in practice researchers
hunt for their own breakthroughs, and replication occurs more slowly than it should,
if at all. 17 Results that attract attention are used and cited and built upon before they
are established beyond doubt. What is accepted as truth becomes, in practice, partly
what it suits the consumer of research for it to be.
Moreover, the individual research publication cannot really be checked. Certainly, the
method can and will be described, but whether that method was properly followed, and
whether the basic data reported -if that is even made available -is an accurate represen-
tation of what was actually found are matters that have to be taken on trust -until repli-
cation occurs. 18 The research claims 'most people think x'; all the reader can respond is 'if
you say so'.
Eventually, in too many cases, the bubble burst, after a replication failed or a team par-
ticipant spoke out and doubt was cast on the validity of the research, and the current
crisis of trust was born. But institutions cannot remedy this by demanding more replica-
tion -unless they want to pay for it, which they do not -so their only way of restoring the
status of research and researchers, and of ensuring that science actually progresses in a
meaningful way and does not descend into a neo-medieval swamp of unproven but theo-
logically attractive theories, is to try and police the process, in practice by imposing
greater obligations on researchers to behave according to codes of good practice and
integrity.
There is something paradoxical, perhaps regrettable, about subjective and personal
factors such as honesty and trust being central to the status of a branch of human activity
that likes to present itself as objective and factual. Nevertheless, the emphasis on the per-
sonal integrity of the researcher is an understandable response to circumstances. 19 From
the perspective of people and institutions who want to be respected, it makes sense for

Piper, 'Science has been in a "replication crisis" for a decade. Have we learned anything? Bad papers are still published.
But some other things might be getting better' [2020] VOX, October 14 2020. https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/
21504366/science-replication-crisis-peer-review-statistics ; Romero 'Philosophy of Science' (n 4).

17 Felipe Romero, 'Novelty versus Replicability: Virtues and Vices in the Reward System of Science' (2017) 84(5) Philosophy
of Science 1031.
18 Sutrop and Lõuk (n 1); Romero 'Philosophy of Science' (n 4)
text.body:
them to devise formulas for displaying their moral worth. Doctors and lawyers also take
oaths and are subject to supervisory bodies and rules. Public status demands public dis-
plays of submission. Hence the UK code, similarly to that of other jurisdictions, defines
research integrity as 'the conduct of research in ways that promote trust and confidence
in all aspects of the research process'. 20
Critiques of integrity codes
The development of codes of integrity has not been without criticism. Some is quite prac-
tical; that there is an over-emphasis on detailed rules, which is bureaucratic and not
always effective, and can even conflict with genuinely ethical practice. 21 This kind of cri-
tique is usually to do with the detailed rules of practice concerning protection of the par-
ticipants in experiments.
There is also concern about the more open and abstract elements of the codes, which
are typically a mix of precise rules concerning experimental practice and general commit-
ments to integrity. 22 These general principles invite the creation of a culture of normative
policing where someone -those on the ethics boards, or the supervisory panels -is able
to determine what is the good and the ethical for the research community. 23 The con-
cerns have been less to do with misuse of this -as yet -but with the very idea of subject-
ing such imprecise and contestable ideas to personal authority. 24 This could smother
diversity regarding conceptions of the moral and the ethical, and inspires the fear that
persons occupying such senior policing roles will become figures in the research commu-
nity who 'must be obeyed'. 25 Codes of integrity with enforcement mechanisms become,
inevitably, mechanisms for creating moral hierarchy. Even without such mechanisms, the
fact of the code invites people to support it publicly, to embrace it, and so to establish
their credentials as those on the good side -with the implication that who disagree
are on the bad.
Finally, there are critiques which are very fundamental, concerned with the fact that
limiting the normative freedom for researchers is also limiting the scope for knowledge
production; is anti-scientific. 26 A response may be that to some extent this is inevitable,
for certain practices are simply abhorrent, and any knowledge that may result from such
unethical experiment is not worth the price. Nevertheless, the recognition that confining
research within generally accepted frames of what is good and right is in some ways pro-
blematic does lead to the conclusion that constraints should not go beyond the necessary
-that an ethics or integrity code should never be a maximal guide, but a minimally intru-
sive outer limit to research.
text.note:
21 Kevin Haggerty, 'Ethics Creep: Governing Social Science Research in the Name of Ethics' (2004) 27 Qualitative Sociology
391; Zachary Schrag, Ethical Imperialism: Institutional Review Boards and the Social Sciences, 1965-2009 (Johns Hopkins
University Press 2017); Spicker 'One Size Fits All (n 14).

23 Malcolm M Feeley, 'Legality, Social Research, and the Challenge of Institutional Review Boards' (2007) 41(4) Law and
Society Review 757; Robert Dingwall, 'Turn off the Oxygen … ' (2007) 41(4) Law and Society Review 787.
26 Schrag 'The Case Against' (n 12); Haggerty (n 21); Rothman (n 6); van den Hoonaard (n 3).
text.body:
What does integrity mean for legal scholars?
Law is different. Traditionally, most legal scholars write a kind of critical commentary on
legal developments, drawing to a greater or lesser extent on extra-legal ideas from phil-
osophy, politics, social science or other fields. 27 Increasingly, there are researchers in law
faculties who do empirical work that would be methodologically recognisable for those
from social and human science faculties. 28 Nevertheless, these are still a minority.
For this latter group, the codes of integrity have the same meaning and relevance as for
other empiricists. They may even be more important: empirical legal studies is still an
emerging branch, and achieving public and academic status may require ostentatiously
visible declarations of allegiance to the accepted norms and methods of research. 29
See; we belong. The convert's tendency towards passion is well-known.
For the traditional legal scholars, however, the codes are largely irrelevant. All the
practical rules about participant protection and data management simply have no appli-
cation to their work. Only the general obligations of honesty, integrity, and so on, are
matters that they might actually have to comply with, along with certain specific rules
on plagiarism, recognition of co-authors, and conflicts of interest.
This paper will not further discuss plagiarism or authorship rules. The principles they
express are hard to object to, but they are not about the content of the research as much
as its attribution to the correct person. They protect careers more than the quality of
knowledge. By contrast, the general obligations to conduct research in an honest and
ethical way, and the rules concerning conflicts of interest, are intended to (i) help guar-
antee better research, and (ii) reassure the public that published research and researchers
can be trusted.
The former, general obligations are not particularly enforced in practice but serve as a
general ideological frame for the codes and the idea of a 'good' researcher that they
embody. It is imaginable though that they could be invoked if a doctrinal lawyer was
involved with criminal or extremist elements or appeared to be driven by a commitment
to generally abhorred values. The conflicts rules by contrast are much more concrete, and
generally require researchers to indicate if they are financially or institutionally involved
with persons or organisations outside their university who might have some kind of
interest in the outcome of their research.
On the whole, there has been no objection by legal scholars to proclaiming agreement
with these, and a certain discussion has developed about the ethical obligations of legal
researchers who may also be part-time lawyers, or have other functions, and the extent to
which these create problematic conflicts, with an emerging consensus on the importance
of transparency. 30
Nevertheless, I suggest that the application of these obligations to legal doctrinal
researchers is harmful to the quality and progress of their work, and rests on a
text.note: 27 Smits (n 5); Jan Vranken, 'Exciting Times for Legal Scholarship' (2012) 2(2) Law and Method 42.

28 See van Gestel and Micklitz (n 10); Daniel Blocq and Maartje van der Woude, 'Making Sense of the Law and Society
Movement' (2018) 11(2) Erasmus Law Review 134; Davies 'The Relationship' (n 10).

30 Stephen Sugarman, 'Conflicts of Interest in the Roles of the University Professor' (2005) 6(1) Theoretical Inquiries in Law
255; David Resnik, The Price of Truth. How Money Affects the Norms of Science (OUP 2007). C.f., on the problems of trans-
parency, George Loewenstein, Sunita Sah and Daylian Cain, 'The Unintended Consequences of Conflict of Interest Dis-
closure' (2012) 307(7) JAMA 669.
text.body:
misunderstanding of what it is they do. Legal scholars are being squeezed into an aca-
demic and institutional space designed for those doing very different work. 31
If the legal academic community shows little resistance to this squeezing, it may be for
several reasons. One no doubt is that for most scholars it has little practical impact on
their work or life -they have no conflicts of interest, as they are currently understood,
and are happy to promise not to lie or cheat or endorse extremism. Another reason,
for some, may be that in a culture of normative conformity it is difficult to speak out.
A certain irony is that arguments against a code of integrity will be better received if
coming from someone who clearly complies with it. Finally, of course, there are career
advantages to simply embracing the codes, particularly for those who participate in
the faculty ethics boards or lead the working groups or discussion panels charged with
disseminating the idea of ethical legal research. A chance to sign up to a Good Agenda
is a low-cost opportunity to promote one's personal career and entrench one's insti-
tutional position. 32 However, even non-opportunist scholars may welcome the general
enhancement in status and reputation that comes from collective commitments to
honesty, transparency, serving the public interest, and so forth. These commitments
encourage respect, rather than scepticism, from the public and other scholars, and
increase the weight that these non-specialist publics will give to their words. That,
however, is precisely the problem.
The nature of legal scholarship
A traditional legal journal article or book draws on legislation and court judgments as its
primary data, and constructs an argument or analysis of them, referring usually to other
scholarship of a similar type and perhaps drawing, in a more or less dilettante kind of
way, on ideas from other disciplines, such as philosophy or political science. 33 It
adopts styles and methods of discourse similar to those used in the courtroom. This is
what fills most of the pages of the most established and widely read legal journals and
as scholarship it has three features which are quite distinctive, particularly by comparison
with most empirical research:
(1) Legal doctrinal writing of this type does not establish facts which are accepted by the
community of legal scholars. 34 Rather, it attempts to make an argument for a certain
point of view, and is evaluated and considered useful according to the nature and
quality of that argument. 35
The argument, however, even if much admired, rarely settles anything. Disagree-
ments between doctrinal lawyers are largely about the interpretation of laws.
However, the indeterminacy of language generally, combined with the variety of pol-
itical and other values which may be brought to bear in deciding what a word or
text.note:
32 Such support requires 'all of the moral fortitude of unconditionally voicing support for motherhood': Haggerty (n 21)
393.
text.body:
phrase does or should mean, ensures that debates in this field rarely conclude, any
more than they do in any other value-laden and politicised field. 36
Of course, there are certain statements of or about the law on which there is con-
sensus, but these are then regarded as banal or trivial, at best stuff to be taught to
undergraduates, but not -because they are so obvious -the object of research.
Research focusses on grey areas, and that, in the context of language and values,
means it is eternally contested. If it is settled -and occasionally questions are -it
is usually because empirical research intervenes. Lawyers can argue forever about
a legislative interpretation, but if empirical research shows the consequences of a
certain meaning, that may impact even on them. 37
The value of such legal scholarship is then in its contribution of ideas and insights,
and perhaps because it leads to empirical research by others. An article is not impor-
tant because it shows X to be true, but because it makes an argument for X that is
original and interesting enough to be worthy of consideration by lawyers or others. 38
(2) The quality of legal scholarship is ensured by debate. 39 An author argues for X, and
someone responds by pointing out all the weaknesses in their argument and
suggesting Y, others intervene, and so on. Legal scholarship proceeds, if it does
proceed, by a dialectic process of engagement and counter argument very similar
to what happens in court. Unlike the empirical sciences, where quality can be main-
tained by ensuring the research process behind the publication is appropriate, there
is no optimal process which can guarantee that published legal research is good. As
an essentially theoretical process, which requires creative leaps towards new
interpretations, ensuring that legal doctrinal researchers approach their research
in a certain way, or with certain methods, will not ensure that they produce persua-
sive or interesting arguments. Rather, the quality of legal scholarship is only main-
tained by critical engagement with what is said.
(3) Closely related to point 2 above: legal doctrinal scholarship is all on the page.
Different people may value a publication differently, according to their personal
values, politics and tastes, but in order to evaluate it all they need is the publication,
some time to read and think, and access to the primary sources it references -which
are invariably public. 40 There is no need to examine data or methods behind the
page, and in no case is it relevant to the evaluation process to know who the
author is, what their personality or ethics or character are, or even who is paying
them. Certainly, it may be interesting, for specialists often know each other, and aca-
demics are not immune to the pleasure of gossip. If a notably weak argument is made
for some currently fashionable aspect of European integration, for example, and the
author is a recipient of a European research award, then it may be hard to resist the
frisson of a moment's moral superiority. However, the argument is not made weaker,
text.note:
36 Rubin (n 9); John Hasnas, 'Back to the Future: From Critical Legal Studies Forward to Legal Realism, Or How Not to Miss
the Point of the Indeterminacy Argument' (1995) 34 Duke Law Journal 84; Nicholas Mignanelli, 'Critical Legal Research:
Who Needs It?' (2020) 112 Law Library Journal 327.

37 Theodore Eisenberg, 'The Origins, Nature, and Promise of Empirical Legal Studies and a Response to Concerns' (2011) 5
University of Illinois Law Review 1713; Davies 'The Relationship' (n 10).
text.body:
or stronger, by that research award. The correlation might seem to tell us something
about the author, but it does not tell us anything about the quality of their work.
In the light of this understanding of what doctrinal legal scholars do, the next two sec-
tions consider the problems of applying integrity and conflicts rules to them and their
work. What is the point, and what is the harm?
Do we need to trust academic lawyers? Should we?
Empirical researchers need to be trustworthy, because the reader cannot check their
methods or data, and cannot assume that anyone else effectively can either. 41 Legal
research, however, because it is all on the page, does not need trustworthy authors.
The major reason for having obligations to act with honesty and integrity, to prevent
researchers from cheating behind the scenes, does not apply.
Nor would it be particularly useful to the reader to know that a legal author is an
honest and trustworthy person, committed to the good of humanity, because there is
no reason to think that these admirable aspects of their personality would increase the
quality of the arguments they produce. A cynic might even suspect the opposite. At
any rate, lacking empirical evidence, the only rational starting point is that character
and argument quality -thus the quality of legal scholarship produced -are unrelated. 42
General integrity obligations applied to lawyers are thus a waste of time, doing nothing
to improve or guarantee the quality of legal doctrinal research. They are not, however, a
harmless irrelevance, for they actually undermine that quality, by encouraging readers
and publics to accept arguments on the basis of trust and personal authority. 43 In build-
ing up the status of the researcher they encourage all those who might be reliant on her
research to replace critical examination, and a presumptive scepticism, with presumptive
trust. 44
This is a gradual process, but when the institutions and personnel of academe publicly
proclaim that their work can be trusted because an ethical approach to research is
respected and policed throughout their fields this will surely have some reputational
effect. That is, indeed, precisely the point, in the empirical sciences where these codes
originate and where trust is so important. However, where doctrinal law is concerned
matters are quite different. The premise that integrity improves quality does not hold,
and, more importantly, accepting it pushes out the factors which do improve quality,
which are scepticism and doubt in the mind of the reader.
Of course, the promotion of the researcher as a person of integrity, deserving of trust,
may be a welcome development for the researcher or her employing institution. It can be
very pleasant to be recognised as an authority and have one's views taken as authoritative
in public discussion. Most people can enjoy being looked up to, at least a little. However,
presumptive scepticism and critical examination are what protects the quality and the
value of legal scholarship, and the more they fade, the more useless and even harmful
such scholarship becomes, turning into no more than complex propaganda from a
text.note: 41 Romero 'Philosophy of Science' (n 4); Wilholt (n 4); Sutrop and Lõuk (n 1).
text.body:
subset of the ruling class -for even if legal academics like to imagine themselves as rebels,
they are socially part of the governing establishment, and even more so if their proclama-
tions are taken as truth. They need to be doubted, vigorously.
It is easy to imagine that the stimulation of personal authority will spread into the
academy itself, so that publications by the great and the good will be accepted more
easily, and critiques less so, and the formation of hierarchy within the scientific discus-
sion process -whether in a conference or an editorial board -will be encouraged. Many
academics -in some countries more than others -will have experienced the situation
where a junior researcher with a good point is silenced by the senior one being corrected,
to prevent their embarrassment. Hierarchy trumps the quality of argument and analysis
here, and such exercises of personal authority are the antithesis of scholarship and the
enemy of intellectual progress. However, they are what the promotion of the legal
scholar as a person of integrity encourages. Certainly, legal academic readers are often
naturally critical ones, and a culture of critique will not be swept away overnight by
an ethics code. However, the promotion of integrity provides another push away from
engagement, and towards status-based research authority. Why do this, when it serves
no good?
These arguments are all a fortiori because the missteps and weaknesses in scholarship
need not have any connection with intention. It is hard to construct a watertight and per-
suasive argument using words, built with the crumbly bricks of imprecise judgments and
legislation coming from political compromise, the sausage-meat of language. A well
intentioned, honest, and ethical scholar may well say things that the next scholar will,
rightly, tear to pieces. Legal scholarship is methodologically closer to philosophy or theol-
ogy than to empirical science, and as in those fields, only a fool thinks that they will settle
an argument for once and for all -or even for a while. 45 Emphasising the integrity of legal
scholars implies that what they do is something more definitive than this, that it is like the
empirical sciences where a well-constructed experiment may lead to finding which is
accepted by all as true. That implication, however, is a fraud on the public.
It is thus essential to the process of constructing legal knowledge that readers and con-
sumers of scholarly arguments approach them critically, even suspiciously, probing them
for their weak points. The only function of public integrity commitments is to try and
dispel this doubt -to replace critical analysis with trust. By contrast, it would be
better for the quality of legal writing if every reader imagined that the author was a dis-
reputable crook whose scholarly reputation it was their mission to destroy -albeit that
there is much to be said for engaging in that destruction politely, but that is another
point.
Conflicts of interest
Rules concerning conflicts of interest can be seen as a specific instance of the general
integrity obligation. However, they are always given particular attention in research
codes, and are where the heart of the matter lies for legal scholars. In practice, while
many academics love a puzzle and want to find the best answer, many also have jobs
on the side with law firms, government, NGOs, or even the judiciary, and there is a

potential conflict of interest between what their non-university employers would like to
see written, and the arguments that the cases and legislation best support. There has been
discussion in the Netherlands and Finland, for example, about the phenomenon of pro-
fessors of tax law with part-time posts as tax lawyers who write and speak in favour of
lower taxes. 46 Are they serving scholarship, or their clients, when they do this? Do we
not need some rules to prevent legal scholarship becoming merely a lobbying forum?
The integrity debate that lives, at least to some extent, in legal academe is about the pos-
ition of scholars who are externally employed, and whose writings align with the interests
of their clients.
The result of this debate is an emphasis on transparency that is now almost consensual
-it must be public who pays the scholar, and who finances their research -reflected in
the codes of conduct, and the ubiquitous journal requirements to declare conflicts of
interest and sources of funding. 47 There are also those who think that academics
should be treated similarly to judges, and external financial connections should not be
allowed at all, or should be restricted, because they undermine the integrity of the scho-
larly process. 48 An academic should undertake to do their best to speak the truth, to make
arguments that they believe to be correct, goes the argument, and they will be deviated
from this path if they are paid by a party with an interest in what they say. It will
inhibit them from voicing inconvenient truths. Universities usually have a concept of
academic freedom, that while they may pay our salaries, they may not tell us what to
write in return for that payment. Even if private employers include analogous clauses
in their contracts, these will never have the same effectiveness. Usually it will be far
easier for them to end their relationship with the academic in the event that it is not
proving satisfactory. Also, if the academic is a practicing lawyer then it will be clients
they have to please, clients who have no obligation at all to maintain their links with a
lawyer who apparently argues in print against their interests. The extra-university
financial relationship creates a genuine pressure to toe the line of the payer.
Nevertheless, even transparency requirements are fairly pointless, and may even be
harmful, because they are once again based on a false conception of what legal scholar-
ship is. 49 They serve primarily to provide false comfort -and so to stand in the way of the
all-important scepticism which is the only meaningful quality control on legal scholar-
ship. 50 For the idea that it is important to reveal, or prohibit, external financial relations
rests on two assumptions: (i) that money influences what legal scholars write; (ii) that
knowing a scholar's influences should change how readers or the public approach
their work. The first may well be true, at least quite often. The second, it will be
argued below, is false.
On the first assumption, it is possible to be brief: it seems very likely that if taking a
certain point of view brings financial advantages, then at least some academics will do
this. That is particularly so because if they work in a certain world they may also be

sitair Weekblad Mare 16/12/21. https://www.mareonline.nl/wetenschap/deze-hoogleraren-strijden-tegen-
belastingontwijking-en-veel-collegas-zijn-daar-niet-blij-mee/ ; Santtu Raitasuo, 'The Conflict of Interest in Tax Scholar-

49 See also Loewenstein, Sah and Cain (n 30).
text.body:
normatively aligned with the other players. A belief that the interests of business, for
example, are important may be their belief too, or at least they may be able to convince
themselves that it is. So it is certainly reasonable to wonder about the motivation of the
scholar who earns on the side.
But does that mean that knowing about this income should change how we view their
work? It may invite an extra alertness, and so could seem harmless at least, a matter
which will be considered more below. However, there are two principled reasons not
to allow our approach, as readers, to be guided by the scholar's financial background.
The simplest one is this; the fact that someone is being paid to make an argument
does not mean it is a bad argument; if we thought that, it would be the end of the
legal process! The challenge in legal doctrinal scholarship is to construct a piece of
work that is persuasive and coherent enough to meet scholarly standards, not to
express one's deepest self. As a reader of such work, we should try to find gaps in the
logic and counter-arguments, but also ideas that can take our own understanding
further. An ideal reader does not however pay attention to who wrote the work, and is
certainly not interested in why -whether it was the product of careerism, instructions
from their project leader, bloody-minded contrarianism, a desire for acceptance in a nor-
matively bounded scholarly community, political ambitions, or financial self-interest.
The questions are not 'who said this and why did they say it?' but 'what did they say,
and does it work?'
The second, more complex but more important argument, is this: the fact that
someone is not being paid does not mean that their scholarly standpoints come from
a disinterested and objective search for truth. 51 That mistake, in fact, is probably more
dangerous than is the influence of the part-timers. On the whole, making a distinction
between legal scholars who earn on the side, and those who don't, turns out to be inco-
herent, because it rests on the idea that there is a neutral way of doing legal scholarship, to
which we should aspire, and from which external commitments pull us away.
For it is common, even the norm, that lawyers write from a certain normative perspec-
tive. They have normative commitments, and these motivate and shape their work. 52
Whether it is a business lawyer sympathetic to the needs of business, or an activist
scholar dedicated to equality, diversity and protection of the vulnerable, or a climate
lawyer who believes passionately in the need for emissions reductions, or the EU
lawyer who considers that the construction of EU law is vital to the wellbeing of the con-
tinent, their normative standpoints are premises for the arguments they make, even
though those premises are not incontestable, and not universally shared. Legal scholars
build arguments on normative foundations that are personal, contestable, and not chal-
lenged in their own work. 53 They do so largely in the scholarly context of communities -
often built around specialist journals -which broadly share their foundations. 54
Some legal writing does not seem to be so agenda driven. There are plenty of thought-
ful, balanced, overviews of the law which seem to describe it in a neutral way, explaining
text.note:
51 Rothman (n 6); PLoS Medicine Editors, 'Making Sense of Non-Financial Competing Interests' (2008) 5(9) PLoS Med e199;
Sandro Galea, 'Typology of Nonfinancial Conflict in Population Health Research' (2018) 108(5) American Journal of Public
Health 631. See also Jeanne Lenzer, 'When is a Point of View a Conflict of Interest?' (2016) 355 British Medical Journal
355:i6194.
52 See generally Rothman arguing 'conflicts' are ubiquitous, Rothman (n 6).
53 Pierre Schlag, 'Pre-Figuration and Evaluation' (1992) 80(4) California Law Review 965.
text.body:
how it works, and considering its merits and demerits from different points of view,
almost like a responsible teacher not wanting to tell their class what to think. But this
methodological choice is also not neutral: how law should be interpreted and how it
works are both contested matters, with some emphasising the importance of text,
others of original intent, of legal context, or of social consequences. No publication
can take account of all perspectives -or at least such publications do not exist. The
'balanced', scholarly, overview usually emphasises the coherence of the law and its prac-
ticality, taking a middle-of-the road common sense and justice kind of approach that is
eminently defensible, and close to the style that judges often adopt. It is not, however, the
only possible approach, nor even a majority one, and as such, not neutral in any sense. 55
It implicitly endorses its style of analysis and interpretation, rather than more revolution-
ary, consciously subversive, or punk styles of law. Its premises are to do with the style of
an argument about law, and the way law should be understood, but they are just as
present, and just as normative and contestable, as those in more overtly political writing.
This makes legal scholarship inherently incomplete. It does not arrive at conclusions
that can be accepted by all, in the way that a chemical experiment may do. It arrives at
conclusions that, if based on good argument, may be persuasive to those who share the
premises of the approach. In this sense, all legal scholarship is advocacy, an academic
form of what lawyers do in court. 56 It takes a side and tries to construct the most persua-
sive argument possible. Typically the legal academic thinks that their approach is the best
one, which the practicing lawyer may not, but that makes no difference to their method,
or the evaluation of what they produce. The judge -whether a gowned one or a sceptical
reader -may be just as persuaded by the paid lawyer as by the pro bono one.
It is thus inherently misguided to try and look for an 'objective' or 'neutral' kind of
legal scholarship, free of uncontested premises. 57 This does not exist, and it is hard to
see in what way it is relevant to know where the premises of the scholarship come
from, whether it is the author's personal moral commitments, or the personal moral
or other commitments of those paying her. 58 To put another person's world view into
legal argument is just as valuable as to express one's own. 59 The business lawyer's argu-
ments are no less valid because they are paid than the migration lawyer's arguments are
invalid because they care. 60
Indeed, one may even go a step further, and say that it is more valuable to represent
another -that the unethical lawyer, in the sense of the one who makes arguments from
premises she does not share -plays a more essential role in developing understanding of
the law than does the ethical one. Partly this is because the wicked argument is the one
text.note:

Apology to Utopia: The Structure of International Legal Argument (Cambridge University Press 2006); Kennedy (n 55).

57 Schlag (n 53); Mignanelli (n 36); Hasnas (n 36); Rothman (n 6); Paul Spicker, 'Ethical Research in Public Policy' in Ron
Iphofen and Dónal O'Mathúna (eds), Ethical Evidence and Policymaking: Interdisciplinary and International Research
(Policy Press 2022) 139.

59 See Koskenniemi critiquing 'authenticity' in Martti Koskenniemi, ''The Lady Doth Protest Too Much'. Kosovo, and the
Turn to Ethics in International Law' (2002) 65(2) Modern Law Review 159.

60 Rothman (n 6); Galea (n 51); See Lenzer (n 51) at 2; C.f. West 'If you are writing in pursuit of justice, you write from the
heart or you don't write at all', Robin West, 'The Ethics of Normative Legal Scholarship' (2018) 101 Marquette Law Review
981, 988.
text.body:
that ultimately makes the good argument stronger: an argument from a perspective that
does not enjoy social consensus, and that is widely seen as dislikeable -such as the
financial self-interest of a particular narrow group -has to be met and rebutted in
order to make opposing positions robust and resilient. Scholarship which is merely an
erudite love-in of the socially concerned contains no critical contest, and will become
flabby and self-satisfied. It is in vanquishing opposing arguments that we develop and
strengthen our own. 61
But secondly, it is also because academia has its own culture and attitudes, and the pol-
itical centre of gravity of the law faculty is quite considerably to the left of wider society,
both socially and economically. Yet surely debate about law should take account of all per-
spectives, and not just be a collective defence of the world view of the academic. The law
professor who speaks on behalf of another, particularly on behalf of a group under-rep-
resented in the university -such as the socially conservative, or the business community
-is therefore doing an essential and noble job, just as they do in court. They should not
be treated as unethical, but rather as a vital player in the game of legal debate.
Integrity as a concession to reality
How much does it all matter? Or to put it another way, how much do the arguments
above, even if they are coherent, actually weigh? For the risks of creating moral hierar-
chies, and displacing critical engagement by person-based assessment, might all seem
a bit abstract, whereas in a concrete situation it is tempting to feel that it does no
harm to know who the author's influences are, and might even be helpful as a kind of
alert that an agenda is being pursued. Perhaps it can then heighten scepticism and cri-
tique, which surely can only be good. Moreover, the course of a debate is not just
influenced by the quality of arguments, but also by their absence. Knowing who pays
may warn us that perhaps some voices are over -or under -represented in the discus-
sion, so that we should not take the dominance of certain views as indicating they are
really the most persuasive. All of us read sometimes beyond our field of specialism,
and precisely here, lacking the expertise to judge as deeply as we would like, we are vul-
nerable to the force of the consensus. The driving forces of that consensus could be good
to know. Disclosure of interests in specific cases may be seductive enough to displace
abstract fears arising from its generalised use.
That apparent pragmatism would be an error. For even if disclosure of interests seems
to provide a kind of insight, it is a selective insight, and that can be more misleading than
helpful. Scrutiny is relative. If funded articles are examined more critically, that entails
necessarily that unfunded ones -the majority in doctrinal legal scholarship -are exam-
ined relatively less so. A certain class of scholarship is given extra examination. However,
it has been argued above that the effects of financial commitments on the quality of scho-
larship are no different from the effects of normative ones: both create a commitment to
an outcome more than a process, and a certain narrowing of the mind. Similar effects, it
was suggested, can arise from calculated career motives. Selective disclosure however
invites us to mistrust the author who is paid, but not the one who has strong normative
views or lively ambition, a position which is utterly incoherent.

It is of course an empirical question how much it has that effect on individual readers,
or on the culture of scholarship: it could even be argued that an awareness of conflicts in
some situations might make us sceptical about research generally. However, the point
here is the selectivity is unjustified and prima facie pushes readers in the wrong direction.
For declaring conflicts of interests, as currently understood, promotes certain kinds of
scholarship over others, without their being any reason to think that this is better or
more objective. The situation might be different if scholars were required to declare
everything; their political views, the views of the heads of their department, their judg-
ment of which opinions are easier to get through peer review, and which styles of scholar-
ship are more likely to lead to promotion or research awards. But, of course, that would
be impossible and chaotic. Any fair and objective analysis of published work thus has to
assume that there are myriad corrupting factors which may have influenced the choice of
argument, and get on with the work of trying to take that argument apart. Selective dis-
closure, by which I mean revealing some kinds of influences but not all, is not a harmless
bit of extra information, but an active distortion of the scholarly world.
Communicating to the public may seem to be a special case. They are important con-
sumers of legal scholarship, when lawyers write for newspapers or speak in the media
about subjects on which they appear to have expertise. But they are not in a position
to engage in deep critical analysis of legal scholarship, and so they need signals on
who can be trusted and when. This is to console the public, but also to keep them
onside -if they perceive academics as untrustworthy, it will have no good consequences
for the funding of universities, or the social status of those academics. In our own self-
preservation, we need to send the right signals. When the public find out that a professor
who appears on talk shows is being paid by X corporation, they will be angry, all my argu-
ments above notwithstanding.
The idea that while transparency and disclosure may be disruptions of the ideal scho-
larly world they are necessary concessions to our public role does have force. Performa-
tive integrity may indeed enhance public trust, as may other behavioural tricks, such as
dressing appropriately, or speaking in earnest, yet measured, tones. If academics play a
part that the public expects, it may improve their public reception.
However, if the integrity rules do not in fact increase the trustworthiness of the
research, as is here argued that they do not, then adopting them to soothe the public
is a manipulation of perceptions, and itself hardly ethical: 62 using integrity as a trick
to deceive the public into thinking academics are more authoritative than they really are.
For, while law professors are sometimes asked to explain something uncontroversial,
as an engineer might be asked to explain the working of an engine, usually they are
invited to give their input in matters of public debate. Should a certain law be
adopted? Is a certain action lawful? In such issues there are always differences of legal
opinion, and it would be regressive if the public were encouraged to simply believe
whichever expert is on display.
Rather, if lawyers are to play a constructive role in public debate then they should be
understood as purveyors of more or less attractive ideas and arguments, not speakers of
truth. 63 The public should be discouraged from seeing them as figures of authority, but

merely as deliverers of a point of view which is worthy of consideration, but not defini-
tive. That places a burden on the media, to present multiple points of view, and it places a
burden on the public, to try and engage with legal debates, and above all, to accept that
the law is often uncertain and unclear, and that an academic lawyer's views are personal
ones, not objective fact. That might not do the status of the law or lawyers much good,
but at least it has the merit of being true.
Conclusion
Doctrinal legal scholarship does not generally provide right answers, and nor does it even
proceed according to universally accepted methods. It consists of normative arguments
about values and the interpretation of words. Together, those arguments help us con-
struct a language for talking about the issues subject to law, and that language can be
both useful and influential in the courtroom, in law-making, and in the world of
social science.
The critical engagement of legal academics with each other's work is what ensures the
quality and precision of that language and helps it to develop. It does not lead to an end to
debates, but to a deepening and broadening of the ways in which different views can be
expressed. To simply trust an article, to accept it uncritically, is not just to construct a
dead end in legal thinking, but to undermine that publication itself and deprive it of
meaning, for the value of legal writing is not in what it proves, but in what it leads to.
The same applies, mutatis mutandis, to the academic herself -to trust her is to miss
her point and make her valueless. The point is to engage and respond.
Law is thus different from empirical science. Whereas the consumer of the latter needs
to trust that the research was carried out and presented honestly, and whereas if this is the
case there is every reason to hope that a little building brick of knowledge has been added
to the world, in the case of legal work neither the person nor the process are relevant to
the value of the product.
To then ask doctrinal legal scholars to declare their commitment to ethics and integ-
rity, with the suggestion that if they do so they and their work will be deserving of more
respect and authority, is to commit a kind of fraud. It makes a dishonest statement which
serves to promote the personal position and comfort of at least some scholars, at the
expense of the quality of scholarship. 64 To suggest that their financial commitments
matter implies that these are somehow different from normative commitments, and
also that the lawyer who speaks for another is somehow less worthy than the lawyer
who speaks for themselves -an abhorrent and unethical view at odds with the essence
of the profession. To suggest that if they are honest and well-intentioned people this
makes their work more valuable is to imply that intelligence and decency are correlated,
a radical and unproven standpoint which if it did turn out to be true would need no
defence -for then the decent would prevail. 65
General integrity obligations, and above all rules on disclosure of interests, should
therefore have no place in the world of non-empirical doctrinal legal scholarship.
They propagate a lie about what law is, and what legal scholars do. The focus should

always be on the words on the page, and those words alone. Anything else is an attempt to
cheat.
